title: Peak of a Mountain

concept.title: Follow the slope
body: A **mountain** array goes strictly up to a peak and then strictly down. The two neighbours tell you on which side of the peak you are standing: if `a[mid] < a[mid + 1]` you are still climbing, so the peak is to the right of `mid`. Otherwise you are on the way down (or on the peak), and the peak is at `mid` or to its left.
This is binary search without a target value: the condition decides the direction by the local shape of the data.

statement: An array of `n` integers (n >= 3) strictly increases up to some index (the peak) and then strictly decreases. The peak is neither the first nor the last element. Print the index of the peak, counting from 0.
outputFormat: Print the index of the peak.
hints: If it is smaller you are going up, so the peak is on the right.
Otherwise the peak is at `mid` or on the left: `hi = mid`.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

# Your code here

explanation: An upward step at `mid` means the peak is to its right, otherwise it is at `mid` or to its left.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

lo, hi = 0, n - 1
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] < a[mid + 1]:
        lo = mid + 1
    else:
        hi = mid
print(lo)
